Why do we resist and resent life’s developmental and obedience tests? By declaring, “I will walk in my own way and do that which is right in my own eyes,” we reject the curriculum of the mortal school in which we are irrevocably enrolled (see Judges 21:25, D&C 1:16). There is only one exit gate leading unto eternal life. Unhappily, only a few find it—but not because God is exclusionary, but because they exclude God from their lives. Even God cannot bring to pass a reconciliation involving only one party.

quotes.text: If brethren dwell together, and one of them die, and have no child, the wife of the dead shall not marry without unto a stranger; her husband's brother shall go in unto her, and take her to him to wife, and perform the duty of an husband's brother unto her. And it shall be, that the firstborn which she beareth shall succeed in the name of his brother which is dead, that his name shall not be put out of Israel (Deut. 25:5-6). The situation in Ruth differs from the "levirate law" codified in Deuteronomy in two important respects: (1) Boaz was clearly not a brother-in-law (Hebrew yabam, Latin levir), and (2) there seems to have been no obligation for either Boaz or "Such a One" to marry Ruth, or it would certainly have come to their attention soon after the arrival of Naomi and Ruth from Moab. However, in one way-which is important for our appreciation of "Such a One's" reaction to Boaz' declaration of his intention to marry Ruth-the remarriage of a childless widow had the same effect as the "levirate": any offspring born to that union would have the right to inherit the property redeemed from Naomi. "Such a One's" initial willingness to redeem the land probably stemmed from his expectation that it would eventually pay for itself. However, the prospect of creating an heir to that property through Ruth, which heir might also be eligible to inherit the property that "Such a One" already owned and would otherwise have fallen to the sons he already had, made the purchase far less appealing. As a consequence, he encouraged Boaz to "redeem thou my right to thyself; for I cannot redeem it" (4:6b). Part of the storyteller's art lies in the suspense in which he kept his listeners for "Such a One's" reaction to Boaz' expression of intention to marry Ruth after "Such a One" had already said that he would redeem the property. Theology and Literary Characteristics The dramatis personae of the book of Ruth are unusual, if not unique, among the narrative writings of the Old Testament: in the entire story there is no king, no royalty, no priests, Levites, Judges, or prophets. All the characters in the story were ordinary people who lived in a town far removed from the centers of power, intrigue, and violence. A similarly striking feature of Ruth is its absence of traditional manifestations of Israelite religion: there is no evidence of the priesthood, nor is there a trace of oracles, visions, dreams, or any of the other usual means of determining God's will. Still, God's "all-causality" was felt continually as he moved in the background of events in the lives of everyday people who possessed the virtues of patience, loyalty, generosity, and trust. It brings the story to its successful and happy resolution. Related to the theme of God's "all-causality" is God's love, which extends to the lives and homes of the simplest of his people, as well as across national borders to traditional enemies of Israel. Ruth is repeatedly referred to as "the Moabitess" in the course of the story (1:22; 2:2, 6, 21; 4:5, 10). Yet, despite the fact that she was a foreigner, and despite the traditional antagonism between Israelites and Moabites (cf. Deut. 23:3-6), through God's love she was permitted to become a mother in Israel and to play an even larger role in God's design as the ancestress of David (4:22) and his greater Son Jesus (Matt. 1:1). Naomi left Bethlehem-Judah with a husband and two sons. When she returned to her home, she was widowed, bereft of both her sons; she brought only a Moabite daughter-in-law with her. Naomi lamented upon her return, "I went out full, and the Lord hath brought me home again empty" (Ruth 1:21). It seemed to Naomi that "the Almighty [had] dealt very bitterly" with her. Nevertheless God, in his never-flagging love, directed the subsequent events which led to the marriage of Ruth and Boaz and the birth of Obed, whom Naomi lovingly held in her bosom and for whom she acted as a nurse at the end of the story. Ruth is a masterpiece of the storytellers' art. With an absolute economy of words, without the use of a "villain" or any real antagonist, without the entrance of kings or priests onto the stage of the story, without the searing emotions or wrenching conflicts of which many stories are made, the teller of Ruth maintains the attention and interest of the listener from beginning to happy conclusion. As long as ordinary people who demonstrate the simple virtues of loyalty, love, and generosity are valued, the book of Ruth will remain a cherished part of our biblical heritage.
quotes.attr: Stephen D. Ricks in Kent P. Jackson and Robert L. Millet, eds., Studies in Scripture, Vol. 3: Genesis to 2 Samuel, p.249-257

quotes.text: The first two chapters in the book of Judges review the situation at the close of Joshua's era and preview the coming cycles of success and failure in Israel's efforts to be God's exemplary nation. Details follow about several of the judges (Heb., shophetim, "leaders, defenders, judges"). Most of them were raised up by the Lord to supplement the priestly leaders in governing Israel, but some who were not raised up by the Lord are also covered. One of them was Jephthah, a somewhat tragic man whom the people themselves summoned to lead them. A different tragic case is Samson, who was called of God even before his birth but seems to have failed his divine calling. The book concludes with a few examples of the extremes of evil that developed during periods of Israel's deep apostasy when "every man did that which was right in his own eyes" (Judg. 17:6; 21:25).
